readme.html:
Tideman voting in C

A command-line program that runs a ranked-pairs (Tideman) election and sets the result beside other voting rules. It started as the Tideman problem in Harvard's CS50 (Problem Set 3) and grew into one C file of 1,323 lines. Beyond the problem set, it can compare voting rules, simulate random elections, and save and load elections.

Each voter ranks every candidate. The program then reports:

  • the ranked-pairs winner, with the locked graph and every head-to-head margin;
  • the Condorcet winner, if there is one, and a check for three candidates that beat each other in a circle;
  • the Borda count winner and an estimated plurality winner (see below);
  • a 0–10 "competitiveness" figure built from the margins.

The methods, as the code implements them

Ranked pairs (Tideman). For every pair of candidates, count how many voters ranked one above the other (record_preferences). Keep each pair one candidate wins outright (add_pairs), sort those wins from the largest margin to the smallest (sort_pairs), then add them to a directed graph in that order, skipping any win whose loser can already reach its winner by following arrows, since locking it would close a cycle (lock_pairs). The winner is the candidate with no arrow pointing at them (print_winner). If one candidate beats every other head to head, ranked pairs always picks them.

Condorcet winner. A candidate who beats every other candidate head to head. There may be none: with three candidates, A can beat B, B beat C and C beat A. The paradox check looks for exactly that pattern among every set of three candidates.

Borda count. On each ballot a candidate scores one point for every candidate ranked below them, so first of three scores 2 and last scores 0. The program sums these from the pairwise table, which gives the same totals as scoring each ballot.

Plurality (estimated). Plurality should count first choices. The program keeps only the pairwise table, not the ballots, so it estimates first-place votes as a candidate's pairwise total divided by the number of opponents. That is the Borda score scaled down, so the "plurality" and Borda winners almost always match. In the demo below the estimate even ties Alice and Bob at 5, while the true first-choice counts are 4, 3 and 2.

Competitiveness. 10 - 20 × (average winning margin ÷ number of voters), clamped to 0–10. Smaller margins give a higher score. It is a figure this program defines, not a standard measure.

Build and run

gcc -o tideman tideman.c

It needs only the C standard library. Small scanf helpers stand in for CS50's get_int and get_string, so the CS50 library is not needed. Built and run with gcc 13.3 on Ubuntu 24.04, where gcc prints one format-overflow warning about the date string.

./tideman Alice Bob Charlie      # election name, number of voters, then each voter's ranking
./tideman -load demo_election.dat  # reprint the results of a saved election
./tideman -i                     # menu: load an election, or simulate elections
./demo.sh                        # scripted 9-voter election; build ./tideman first

Candidate names are single words (at most 15 candidates). An unknown name at a rank prompt asks again. At the end the program offers to save the election to a file.

demo.sh pipes a fixed election into ./tideman and writes test_output.txt (the full results), demo_election.dat (the saved election), load_test.txt and interactive_test.txt.

Simulation

Simulation runs from the menu and uses the candidates of a loaded election (three or more). After ./demo.sh has written demo_election.dat:

printf '2\ndemo_election.dat\n3\n1000\n4\n' | ./tideman -i

Each simulated election has 10 to 100 voters, and each voter's ranking is a random shuffle of the candidates. For every election it records the winner under each method and whether a Condorcet winner exists. At the end it prints how often each candidate won under each method, the share of elections with no Condorcet winner, and the average competitiveness. The "agreement" lines compare how often each method picked each candidate across all runs, not whether two methods picked the same winner in the same election, so they are an upper bound. The random generator is seeded from the clock, so numbers change from run to run.

Example: the demo election

demo.sh casts these nine ballots:

Voter 1st 2nd 3rd
1 Alice Bob Charlie
2 Alice Bob Charlie
3 Bob Alice Charlie
4 Charlie Alice Bob
5 Alice Charlie Bob
6 Bob Charlie Alice
7 Alice Bob Charlie
8 Bob Alice Charlie
9 Charlie Bob Alice

Head to head, Alice beats Bob 5–4 (voters 1, 2, 4, 5, 7), Alice beats Charlie 6–3 and Bob beats Charlie 6–3. Sorted by margin, the program locks Alice → Charlie, Bob → Charlie, then Alice → Bob. None closes a cycle, nothing points at Alice, and she wins. Part of test_output.txt:

═══ TIDEMAN METHOD WINNER ═══
🏆 TIDEMAN WINNER: Alice

═══ VOTING METHOD COMPARISON ═══
Plurality Winner: Alice
Borda Count Winner: Alice
Condorcet Winner: Alice

═══ PREFERENCE MATRIX ═══
(Row candidate preferred over column candidate)

               Alice     Bob Charlie
Alice              -       5       6
Bob                4       -       6
Charlie            3       3       -

═══ LOCKED PAIRS GRAPH ═══
(Arrows show locked preferences)

Alice → Bob (margin: 1)
Alice → Charlie (margin: 3)
Bob → Charlie (margin: 3)

═══ MARGIN ANALYSIS ═══
Alice beats Charlie by 3 votes (33.3%)
Bob beats Charlie by 3 votes (33.3%)
Alice beats Bob by 1 votes (11.1%)
Smallest margin: 1 votes
Largest margin: 3 votes

Election Competitiveness Score: 4.81/10.0

The Borda totals are Alice 11, Bob 10 and Charlie 6. The competitiveness is 10 − 20 × ((1 + 3 + 3) ÷ 3 ÷ 9) = 4.81.

Saved election format

Plain text: the line ELECTION_DATA, the election name, the date, the number of candidates, the number of voters, one candidate name per line, then the pairwise table one row per line. Loading rebuilds the pairs and the locked graph from the table. The ballots themselves are not saved.

Known limits

  • Running fewer than 10 simulations crashes with a floating-point exception: the progress check divides by num_simulations / 10, which is 0.
  • Menu option 1 ("Run New Election") is not implemented; it prints a note and returns to the menu.
  • The first character of the election name is dropped (tideman.c line 441 reads one character before the name), so "Student Council Election 2025" is saved as "tudent Council Election 2025".
  • A ballot may name the same candidate twice; the program does not reject it.
  • The functions ending in _optimized (merge sort and a depth-first cycle check) are never called, so "Operations performed" in the performance section is always 0. The complexity lines printed there are formulas, not measurements.
